description:
We are Team Capstone, competing in the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge under the Rajshahi local event!

Our Team Skills: Web Development, Writing & Communications, Satellites, and Space Weather.
summary:
EarthScope is an interactive web app that turns NASA Earth-observation data into evidence people can trust. As a “trend detective” for Bangladesh, it uses NASA POWER, MODIS, GPM IMERG and GRACE data for all 64 districts from 2001 to 2025. Users choose an environmental variable and time period, then explore trends region by region.

It separates real long-term change from noise by estimating the rate of change with Sen’s slope and testing significance with the Mann-Kendall test. It also shows data coverage and uncertainty, compares regions, and offers a machine-learning forecast validated against simple baselines. A methods panel explains sources and limitations, and results can be exported.

This matters because a rising line on a chart doesn’t show whether a change is real or how it varies by place. EarthScope helps farmers, students, researchers and the public move from what the data appears to show to what the evidence supports.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

EarthScope is an interactive web app that turns 25 years (2001-2025) of NASA Earth-observation data into evidence people can verify. Raw satellite data and climate models produce huge volumes of numbers, and a simple rising line on a chart can mislead. It doesn’t show whether a change is physically real, statistically significant, persistent over time, or specific to one area. We use Bangladesh, one of the world’s most climate-vulnerable countries, as the case study, covering all 64 districts.

  • Robust trend detection: Instead of ordinary least squares, which extreme monsoons and heatwaves can distort, we estimate the annual rate of change with the Theil-Sen estimator (breakdown point of about 29.3%). We test significance with the Mann-Kendall test, using exact tie corrections and Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control across many tests.
  • Dynamic Window Scrubber: Users switch between 10-, 15-, 20- and 25-year windows to see how short-term noise can mimic false warming or cooling.
  • Mirror Finder: It automatically finds district pairs with opposite trends, such as aquifer drawdown in the northwestern Barind tract versus saturation in the northeastern Haor wetlands, and explains the likely climatological drivers.
  • Zarr Explorer: It animates 300 months of gridded NASA data (MODIS NDVI, GPM IMERG precipitation, GRACE terrestrial water storage) and extracts a time series for any pixel on click.
  • Bilingual narration: An automated agent writes plain-language summaries in English and Bangla. A verification layer checks every number in them against the backend calculations.

What benefits does it have?

  • From “apparent trend” to “supported evidence”: Every estimate comes with its p-value, Z-score, 95% confidence interval and data-coverage metrics.
  • Transparent provenance: Every number traces back to a NASA mission (POWER/MERRA-2, MODIS Terra/Aqua, GPM IMERG, GRACE/GRACE-FO). Users can export GeoJSON/CSV and inspect the raw API responses.
  • Fast and offline-capable: Pre-indexed Parquet and Zarr stores return queries in under 50 ms, with no cloud dependency or vendor lock-in.
  • Accessible: Complex statistics are explained in clear language in both Bangla and English.

What is the intended impact?

  • Farmers and agricultural extension officers: They can spot real decade-scale drying or monsoon shifts across agro-ecological zones, which informs planting schedules and drought-tolerant crop choices.
  • Students and educators: It works as a hands-on lab for seeing how sample length changes statistical conclusions, which teaches rigor over confirmation bias.
  • Researchers and journalists: They get a reproducible, auditable toolkit for checking local climate claims.
  • Policy makers and disaster planners: They get objective regional evidence on groundwater depletion and flash-flood risk to guide infrastructure investment.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

  • Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Uvicorn.
  • Scientific computing: NumPy and SciPy (custom vectorized Mann-Kendall and Theil-Sen implementations), Pandas and PyArrow (Parquet), Zarr and Xarray (gridded data).
  • Machine learning: Scikit-learn Ridge regression with harmonic seasonal features and autoregressive lags, validated on time-ordered splits against naive persistence and Holt-Winters baselines.
  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3 (black/yellow/white theme with dark and light modes), vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), Leaflet.js for maps, Chart.js for time series and confidence envelopes.
  • GIS data: HDX/OCHA and GADM Bangladesh district boundaries, with CARTO Positron and Dark Matter basemaps.
  • Development and deployment: Google Antigravity / Gemini CLI, Docker, Git/GitHub, deployed on Render’s free tier (0.1 CPU, 512 MB RAM).

How is your project creative?

  • Conclusion sensitivity: Most climate dashboards show one static line. Our Window Scrubber lets users see how changing the start year can flip a conclusion, so they learn critical thinking by interacting.
  • Mirror Finder: Rather than looking at districts one by one, it compares district pairs to find hidden opposing patterns across micro-climates.
  • Verified narration: Many tools feed data to an LLM that can invent numbers. EarthScope uses deterministic statistical narration plus a layer that checks that every stated figure matches the calculated results.
  • Built-in science literacy: Terms such as Theil-Sen slope, Mann-Kendall Z-score, p-value, GRACE Mascon and MODIS NDVI link to authoritative references, so the app also works as a self-guided learning tool.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Resistance to outliers: Monsoon climates have extreme storms and heatwaves, so we chose rank-based, non-parametric statistics that a single anomalous event can’t distort.
  • Bandwidth and digital inclusion: Rural areas and schools in Bangladesh often have limited connectivity. We used client-side memoization, compressed Parquet files and a touch-first responsive design that works on budget smartphones.
  • Language inclusivity: Every card, tooltip, metric and summary has a native Bangla translation, so affected communities can use it directly.
  • Ethical communication: ML forecasts always show caveats and prediction intervals, and the app avoids causal claims and alarmist warnings.
